title: TB7-06912
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Nigeria and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Nigeria and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant is requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the RPD's negative determination and find that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. The Appellant has requested to submit new evidence and has requested an oral hearing.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),1 the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. This appeal is allowed. Background

The Appellant alleges that she resided in South Africa from 2011 to 2015. While she initially went to South Africa to study, she alleges she was unable to do so because her father ran into financial difficulties. However, while she was in South Africa, she alleges that she started dating XXXX XXXX (hereinafter "Mr. XXXX"), a young Nigerian man. In late 2015, they agreed to get married, but the Appellant did not inform her family immediately because she wanted Mr. XXXX to get permission from her father.

In XXXX 2015, the Appellant and Mr. XXXX returned home to Nigeria. The Appellant alleges that when she returned home, her father informed her that he agreed that she would marry XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (hereinafter "Mr. XXXX"), a much older man and prominent politician and former police officer in Nigeria. She claims that her father promised her to Mr. XXXX because her father ran into financial difficulties and Mr. XXXX was financially supporting her family and paid her school fees. When the Appellant told her father about Mr. XXXX and that she wanted to marry him instead, she claims her father refused because Mr. XXXX is Christian and she is Muslim, and also because he already agreed that Mr. XXXX would marry her and he had already accepted the bride price. The Appellant alleges that she told Mr. XXXX that she did not want to marry him, and that he became angry, but a wedding date was set anyway. The Appellant and her current husband also offered to pay back the bride price and the funds owed to Mr. XXXX, but this was refused because her father promised the Appellant to Mr. XXXX. The Appellant also states that Mr. XXXX made a complaint to the police, but they refused to take the complaint after learning it was against Mr. XXXX.

In XXXX 2016, the Appellant and Mr. XXXX eloped and were married in Ikeja. Subsequently, the Appellant and Mr. XXXX made arrangements with an agent to come to Canada. They obtained U.S. visas and left Nigeria for Chicago in XXXX 2016. They resided in the U.S. for approximately five months, awaiting the agent's assistance to bring them to Canada. In early XXXX 2016, the Appellant states that she and her husband had a fight and that he left the apartment. At the time of her RPD hearing, she alleged that she had yet to hear from Mr. XXXX since their fight in XXXX 2016. Shortly after their fight in XXXX 2016, the agent returned to the apartment and the Appellant made her way to Canada. Further details are provided in her Basis of Claim (BOC) Form, and her testimony at the RPD hearing.2 The RPD's Decision

The Appellant had a refugee determination hearing on December 15 and December 20, 2016. In a written decision issued on March 30, 2017, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD panel found the Appellant lacking in credibility and subjective fear. Therefore, the RPD concluded that the Appellant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground, or that she would not personally be subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or a danger of torture upon return to Nigeria.

For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, the RAD applies the standard of correctness in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Huruglica.3 In assessing findings involving the credibility of oral testimony, the RAD may apply the modified standard of reasonableness in situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage.4 Unless otherwise stated in the reasons, the RAD uses the correctness standard on all findings and will consider the overall refugee determination on a standard of correctness, even where the RAD has deferred on some or all findings. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

In support of her appeal, the Appellant proposes six documents as new evidence: 1) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX, dated 12 June 2017;5 2) Basis of Claim Narrative, XXXX XXXX XXXX, undated;6 3) Photographs of Appellant and her husband, undated;7 4) Medical Letter of Dr. XXXX XXXX, printed 19 April 2017;8 5) Provisional Offer of Admission, XXXX College, dated 25 April 2017;9 and, 6) Revised Letter, XXXX Immigrant Women's Centre, dated 1 May 2017.10

Evidence from the person who is the subject of the appeal is only admissible on appeal if it meets one of the statutory conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, namely that it arose after, or was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time the claim was rejected. If one of these conditions is met, the RAD will then consider if the evidence is credible, relevant, and new as endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh.11 Affidavit of XXXX XXXX and Mr. XXXX BOC Narrative

The affidavit of XXXX XXXX and Mr. XXXX BOC Narrative, indicate that Mr. XXXX made an appointment at Ms. XXXX law firm in order to initiate a refugee claim in Canada in early May 2017. When Mr. XXXX met with the lawyer, the lawyer noted that his story sounded similar to that of the Appellant, who had met with the law firm in April 2017, in order to appeal her negative RPD decision. Although the Appellant did not retain Ms. XXXX law firm for her appeal, the lawyer who met with Mr. XXXX was able to confirm that the individual who came to their office in April 2017 was his wife. As a consequence, the Appellant was able to reunite with Mr. XXXX at the law firm after not seeing each other since he left her in Chicago in XXXX 2016. In his BOC narrative, Mr. XXXX explains that he left the Appellant in Chicago because he was informed by the agent that he did not pay enough money to bring them both to Canada. As a result, Mr. XXXX decided to leave her so that the Appellant would not refuse to go to Canada without him.

The Appellant submits that she could not have provided Mr. XXXX BOC narrative at the time of her hearing because she had no information about her husband's whereabouts at the time of her hearing. She also argues that Mr. XXXX BOC contradicts many of the RPD's findings, including that she embellished the existence of her husband. She submits this evidence establishes that they are married, and that it provides a clear account for why Mr. XXXX stayed in the U.S. and sent the Appellant with the agent alone.

The RAD accepts the affidavit of Ms. XXXX and Mr. XXXX BOC narrative as new evidence. At the time of rejection, the Appellant did not know of Mr. XXXX whereabouts. It was not until May 2017 that she learned he was in Canada. In addition, the BOC narrative appears to be new, relevant and credible. The BOC narrative is relevant, as it corroborates many of the Appellant's allegations of her claim, and also contradicts the RPD's finding that Mr. XXXX does not exist and was an embellishment by the Appellant. It is also on its face credible, because it is accompanied by an affidavit by a licensed lawyer, attesting to the events about how the Appellant and Mr. XXXX were reunited in Canada. Therefore, I find the affidavit of Ms. XXXX and Mr. XXXX BOC narrative are admissible as new evidence under 110(4). Photographs, Medical Letter & Revised Letters

The Appellant submits that these documents are admissible because: she did not know that she was supposed to submit pictures of Mr. XXXX; the medical letter was not available at the time of her hearing and this shows she suffers from depression and anxiety due to the traumatic events; and, the revised letters were not available because she contacted XXXX College and the XXXX Immigrant Women's Centre (RIWC) after the hearing to correct errors in the letters.

I reject the photographs, parts of the medical letter, and the revised letters as new evidence. The Appellant states that these documents were not available at the time of the RPD hearing; however, this is not the test to be met. Rather, it is the date of the RPD's decision that matters. In this case, the Appellant was represented by experienced counsel and she provided photographic evidence of Mr. XXXX. The onus is on her to establish her claim and she could reasonably have been expected in her circumstances to have provided this evidence at the time the RPD rejected her claim. The existence of Mr. XXXX was clearly in issue and the Appellant fails to provide any explanation for why she could not have submitted such photographs before the RPD rejected her claim on March 30, 2017. She had plenty of time to submit such evidence and the photos; and therefore, I find the photos are inadmissible under 110(4).

With respect to the medical letter, I note that it refers to assessments conducted with her doctor on XXXX XXXX, 2016, as well as on XXXX XXXX, 2017. These assessments were completed before the RPD rendered its decision on March 30, 2017, and she provides no reason why she could not have provided these assessments prior to rejection. Therefore, these assessments are inadmissible pursuant to subsection 110(4). However, the medical assessments conducted on XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2017 post-date the RPD's decision and were unavailable at the time of rejection. Furthermore, they are relevant to her mental health and the RPD's consideration of her psychological report. Finally, they appear on their face to be credible as they are print-outs from her doctor at the XXXX Community Health Centre.

In regard to the revised letters from XXXX College and RIWC, these are inadmissible. These issues were put to the Appellant at her RPD hearing, and she would not have been caught off-guard by the RPD findings at the time her claim was rejected. She provides no information why she could not have provided these revised documents prior to March 30, 2017, considering she had more than three months to obtain such documents. In addition, the Appellant is responsible for her evidence and she speaks English. Therefore, it was incumbent on her to review the evidence she submitted to ensure it did not contain any errors and she had ample time to make any necessary corrections. As a result, the revised documents from Boston College and the RIWC are inadmissible under subsection 110(4). Application to Submit Additional Documents (Rule 29 Application)

The Appellant submits an application under Rule 29 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules for the admission of documents not previously provided. The Appellant requests to submit the RPD's decision in her husband's case, wherein he was accepted as a person in need of protection under 97(1) of the IRPA.12

Rule 29 allows the Appellant to make an application to provide a document not previously provided. Such an application must include an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.13 In determining the application, the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including: the relevance and probative value of the document, any new evidence the document brings to the appeal, and whether the Appellant could have, with reasonable effort, provided the document with the Appellant's Record.

The Appellant argues that Mr. XXXX positive decision from the RPD could not have been provided at the time of the Appellant's hearing because at the time of the Appellant's hearing, Mr. XXXX was not in Canada and had not made a refugee claim at that time. She submits that the document is highly relevant because both Mr. XXXX and the Appellant fear persecution on the same grounds. Furthermore, she submits that it is probative of the Appellant's claim because the legitimacy of her relationship with Mr. XXXX was found not credible by the RPD. In addition, the RPD found Mr. XXXX credible in his story and that the country conditions in Nigeria supported his allegations.

I accept the Appellant's Rule 29 application, and I find Mr. XXXX RPD decision is admissible as new evidence. Although the Appellant argues that it was not available at the time of her hearing, this is not the relevant point in time. Rather, Mr. XXXX RPD decision was not mailed out until August 17, 2017, which post-dates the time the Appellant's Record was submitted. Therefore, it was not available at the time the Appellant's appeal record was perfected. In addition, Mr. XXXX RPD decision is relevant and probative as it establishes that allegations that are substantially similar to the Appellant's were accepted as credible by the RPD. As a result, I accept the Rule 29 application and I find the RPD decision of Mr. XXXX is admissible as new evidence under subsection 110(4). Request for an Oral Hearing

The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.14

In this appeal, the Appellant's new evidence pertains to her husband's positive refugee claim, which demonstrates that the facts upon which her claim was based were accepted as credible by the RPD. For the reasons below, and based on this new evidence, the RAD also accepts the Appellant's allegations as credible on a balance of probabilities. The RAD is able to make this determination based on the RPD record and the new evidence under 110(4) and without an oral hearing. Therefore, the RAD chooses not to hold an oral hearing in this case.

The Appellant argues the following issues in her appeal, which I have reorganized for clarity: 1) The new evidence invalidates the RPD's decision; 2) The RPD erred in making a number of unsupported implausibility findings; 3) The RPD erred by failing to apply the Gender Guideline and Vulnerable Person Guideline, as well as the country conditions evidence about victims of gender violence in Nigeria; and, 4) The RPD erred in its subjective fear assessment.15 ANALYSIS New Evidence and Credibility The Appellant's Argument Knowledge of Husband and the Marriage Certificate

The Appellant argues that the new evidence establishes that the RPD erred when it concluded that Mr. XXXX was an embellishment created to pursue her claim and found that she was not married. Rather, she claims the new evidence shows that they are married and that it corroborates her allegations of persecution stated in her narrative and in her testimony.16 The Appellant continues by arguing that the RPD erred by finding that she possessed a lack of knowledge of Mr. XXXX because she was not sure about the date when her husband graduated and whether he had a graduation ceremony. She submits she provided a reasonable explanation of her lack of knowledge, that being, their relationship did not become serious yet and in her culture women do not probe into men's affairs. The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred in its treatment of the marriage certificate when it found it was not credible because it stated Mr. XXXX occupation was business management, rather than I.T.17

I agree with the Appellant's argument and find the RPD erred. I find there is sufficient credible evidence in the record to establish that the Appellant is married to Mr. XXXX. I agree with the Appellant that she provided a reasonable explanation for her lack of detail about not knowing when Mr. XXXX finished school and his graduation ceremony, considering they were not in a serious relationship at that time and she is accustomed to not probing into men's affairs. The Appellant could recall that he completed his education in 2013, but she did not remember the exact date he finished school. She further stated that he started working in I.T. at a company named XXXX in 2014, for nearly two years until they left South Africa and returned to Nigeria. In addition, I find the RPD was microscopic in its assessment of the marriage certificate. I note that although it states he is in business management on the certificate, rather than in an I.T. job, at her hearing the Appellant stated he worked in management at a merchandise company as an IT agent. I further note that she offered this information about a management role, before the RPD pointed out to her that the marriage certificate says his occupation is business management and not IT. I find that the fact that the marriage certificate says he is in business management, does not exclude that he could also work in IT, considering she indicated beforehand that he worked in management at a merchandise company. Therefore, I find the RPD erred in its lack of knowledge finding and its assessment of the marriage certificate. These findings are not supported by the evidence in the record.

Furthermore, although I am not bound by the decision of the RPD with respect to the Appellant's husband, I find it warrants some weight in this appeal to establishing that the Appellant and Mr. XXXX are married to each other. The BOC narrative of Mr. XXXX and his positive RPD decision corroborates the Appellant's allegations that they are married. These were facts found credible by the RPD in Mr. XXXX claim. It is for this reason, as well as the otherwise credible evidence of the Appellant, such as her knowledge of Mr. XXXX, their relationship, and the marriage certificate in the record, that I find that the Appellant and Mr. XXXX are married, on a balance of probabilities. Other Credibility Findings

The RPD found that the Appellant was not credible about her time in South Africa and she was inconsistent with three pieces of her corroborating documents. I find these are not sufficient to maintain the RPD's negative credibility findings for the following reasons. First, the findings about her time in South Africa are not core to her allegations of risk due to forced marriage, and its findings about the inconsistencies in the documentation were mostly microscopic. In particular, I note that the letter from the YMCA stating "she landed in Canada", as opposed to coming to Canada via truck, is not a significant inconsistency. While I agree with the RPD in its finding with the inconsistency in the letter from Riverdale Immigrant Women's Centre (RIWC), I disagree with its treatment of her mother's affidavit. The RPD should have considered what her mother's affidavit does say, rather than what it does not say. While I agree that it would have been helpful for the affidavit to state when her mother learned of the forced marriage, this does not discount the uncontradicted evidence in the affidavit, which otherwise supports the Appellant's allegations that she is being forced to marry Mr. XXXX. Therefore, I find the RPD erred and I find that its credibility findings are insufficient to sustain its conclusion that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

Setting these credibility findings aside, I note that the Appellant was otherwise consistent regarding her core allegations once she returned to Nigeria, such as when she was told she would have to marry Mr. XXXX, the reasons why, and the chronology of events that occurred thereafter. The RPD takes no issue with this testimony and evidence. Based on my review of the record, I find she was consistent in her testimony, in both content and chronology, with her BOC, as well as her other supporting evidence about her core allegations pertaining to the forced marriage to Mr. XXXX. These allegations were also consistent with those alleged by her husband in his BOC and which were accepted by the RPD in his claim. Therefore, I find the Appellant was a credible witness on a balance of probabilities about her core allegations of having to marry Mr. XXXX, a well-known politician in Nigeria, and a former police officer, following her father's financial difficulties. On this latter point, I note that the RPD accepted that Mr. XXXX does exist. Well-founded Fear of Persecution

The Appellant's allegations are objectively supported by the documentary evidence. Mr. XXXX is a well-known Nigerian politician who is also a former police officer and former Governor of XXXX State. The Appellant provided documentation indicating that he may have multiple wives and his treatment of political adversaries, as well as information about his political prominence, and a Human Rights Watch report commenting on his corrupt practices as Governor of XXXX State beginning in 2007.18

The country condition documents are consistent with the Appellant's allegations that she will face a risk from Mr. XXXX if she returns to Nigeria, because of forced marriage. Documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria establish that girls and young women in Nigeria are sometimes forced by family members to marry persons they don't want to marry, particularly when cultural conditions are involved. Item 5.7 provides several factors for decision makers to consider in assessing the credibility of a forced marriage claim. The Appellant's family situation is similar to the profile listed in this document, with the exception of the fact that most of the girls who are forced into marriages are in the north rather than the south, where she's from. Specifically, her family has money issues; her father owed money to Mr. XXXX; and her family is Muslim. These factors in her personal history are consistent with the objective documentation about the traditional background for many girls who are forced into unwanted, family arranged marriages.

The country condition evidence also indicates that the men that young women are forced to marry are usually old, and the consequences of refusal are up to family members and can begin with neglect and ostracism, but in other cases can become very dangerous. This is consistent with the Appellant's claim that Mr. XXXX is approximately 50 years her senior, her family is Muslim, her father was in financial difficulty and accepted the bride price. With regard to refusing a forced marriage, item 5.7 indicates that a woman's ability to refuse depends on factors such as education and income levels and that refusing a forced marriage could be dangerous for the victim; there are reports of women facing death, bodily mutilation, domestic violence and rape for attempting to escape from their husbands and according to one source, many girls who are forced to marry are suicidal.

I also accept that the practice of forced marriage still operates in Nigeria despite many laws to prevent it because Nigeria has many customary laws that provide institutional support for such practices, and because even though steps were taken to implement and enforce the laws meant to prevent it, forced marriage remains a problem. The NDP for Nigeria further states that there is a prevalence of impunity in Nigeria.19 With respect to the Appellant's husband in particular, I note that the RPD found credible that Mr. XXXX brother was beaten and attacked by Mr. XXXX men in a case of mistaken identity. Mr. XXXX testified that Mr. XXXX even visited his brother in hospital to admit to the mistake and to learn about his whereabouts. Despite admitting what had happened, it appears that Mr. XXXX did not fear any repercussions for attacking Mr. XXXX brother, because of the pervasiveness of impunity in Nigeria. Moreover, Mr. XXXX has recently switched parties and continues to be politically active and seeks political office in Nigeria. Therefore, I find that Mr. XXXX reach is extensive, powerful, and influential throughout Nigeria.

Furthermore, I find there is no state protection or internal flight alternative available to the Appellant, given the political power, reach and influence of Mr. XXXX, as well as considering the prevalence of impunity in Nigeria, and the fact that the Appellant and her husband attempted to make a complaint to the police about Mr. XXXX, but the police refused to take the complaint when they learned who the complaint was against.

Finally, while I am not bound by the RPD's decision on the Appellant's husband's claim, her husband's claim was based on the same facts as those alleged by the Appellant. Considering the above credibility assessment, the objective evidence, as well as the fact that the Appellant's husband has been accepted a person in need of protection based on the same allegations as the Appellant, I find the Appellant faces more than a mere possibility of persecution based on her membership in a particular social group, as a young woman forced to marry Mr.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee, as she has a well-founded fear of persecution on the basis of her membership in a particular social group, as a woman being forced into marriage. This appeal is allowed. (signed) "G. Erauw" G. Erauw February 12, 2018 Date 1 Paragraph 111(1)(b), Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c.27.
